title: Acute renal effects of the GLP-1 receptor agonist exenatide in overweight type 2 diabetes patients: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

citation.title: Acute renal effects of the GLP-1 receptor agonist exenatide in overweight type 2 diabetes patients: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial

printed_heading.text: ARTICLE Acute renal effects of the GLP-1 receptor agonist exenatide in overweight type 2 diabetes patients: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial Lennart Tonneijck1 & Mark M. Smits1 & Marcel H. A. Muskiet1 & Trynke Hoekstra2,3 & Mark H. H. Kramer1 & A. H. Jan Danser4 & Michaela Diamant1 & Jaap A. Joles5 & Daniël H. van Raalte1 Received: 15 December 2015 /Accepted: 1 March 2016 /Published online: 1 April 2016 # The Author(s) 2016. This article is published with open access at Springerlink.com

what_it_measured.text: Abstract Aims/hypothesis This study aimed to investigate the acute renal effects of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) exenatide in type 2 diabetes patients.
Study endpoints The primary endpoint of this study was exenatide-induced change in GFR compared with placebo [11].

dose.text: The intravenous solution contained 46 ml of NaCl solution (154 mmol/l) and 4 ml of the participant’s blood (to prevent binding of the study drug to the infusion material), with either 10 μg exenatide (AstraZeneca, London, UK) or an equivalent volume of NaCl solution 154 mmol/l (placebo).

route.text: Because exenatide–placebo pens for subcutaneous administration were not available, the study drug was administered intravenously, thereby allowing blinding of both participants and study personnel.

endpoint.text: GFR (primary endpoint) and effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) were determined by inulin and paraaminohippurate clearance, respectively, based on timed urine sampling.
Secondary outcomes included all other (intra-)renal haemodynamic variables, renal handling of sodium, potassium and urea, and renal damage markers.
Study endpoints The primary endpoint of this study was exenatide-induced change in GFR compared with placebo [11].

reported_results.text: Exenatide increased FENa, FEK, urine osmolality and pH, while FEU, urinary flow and free water clearance were decreased (all p < 0.05).
Exenatide increased RA (p < 0.05), but did not change RE.
Exenatide (n = 24) did not affect GFR (mean difference +2 ± 3 ml min−1 1.73 m−2, p = 0.489), ERPF, FF, ERVR or PGLO, compared with placebo (n = 28).
Compared with placebo, exenatide did not change urinary glucose, albumin, NGAL or KIM-1 excretion (p > 0.05) (Table 2).
Exenatide infusion increased the heart rate (HR) by 7 ± 1 bpm (p < 0.001).
During exenatide infusion, ERVR tended to increase by 0.018 ± 0.009 mmHg l−1 min−1 (p = 0.065).
